### Animals

Experiments were performed using both male and female compound heterozygous crosses of OMP-IRES-tTA (Jackson Laboratory stock #017754) (Yu et al., 2004) and tetO-GCaMP6s (Jackson Laboratory stock #024742) (Wekselblatt et al., 2016) mice aged 2–6 months. Mice were housed up to 5 per cage on a 12 hr light/dark cycle with food and water available ad libitum. All procedures were performed following the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the University of Utah Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. (IACUC protocols #19–06007, 19–06008).

### Olfactometry

Odorants were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich, TCI America, Bedoukian Research, or ICN Biomedicals. Liquid dilutions of odorants were prepared to achieve target delivery concentrations of approximately 0.1, 1, 10, 100, or 1000 pM (within an order-of-magnitude) using 1:10 and 1:100 serial dilutions. Non-amine odorants were diluted in caprylic/capric medium chain triglyceride oil (C3465, Spectrum Chemical Mfg. Corp.) within ~1 week of experiments; amine odorants were freshly diluted in water immediately prior to each experiment to minimize odorant oxidation. Trace quantities of Sudan Black B were included in all dilutions to facilitate visual confirmation of olfactometer loading. Diluted odorants were delivered in vapor phase using a custom-built olfactometer equipped with end-stage eductor and operating with 8 L/min charcoal-filtered carrier stream, 30 kPa delivery pressure, 5 cm olfactometer-to-mouse distance, and 2-s long delivery (Burton et al., 2019). A fan at the rear of the animal removed odorants after presentation. Odorants were delivered independent of inhalation timing in pseudorandom order, typically in sets of 12 odorants, with 3–5 trials per odorant and 8–10 s inter-trial interval. Eductors were washed with non-scented Alconox detergent and thoroughly rinsed with ethanol and water in between odorant sets to minimize possible odorant adsorption and inter-trial contamination.

### Imaging

Mice were initially anesthetized with intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital (50 mg/kg) and subcutaneous injection of chlorprothixene (12.5 mg/kg). Subcutaneous injection of atropine (0.5 mg/kg) was further given to minimize mucus secretions and maintain nasal patency. A double tracheotomy was performed as described (Eiting and Wachowiak, 2018), and anesthesia was subsequently maintained by ~0.4–0.5% isoflurane delivered in pure O2 to the descending tracheal tube while artificial inhalation (150 ms duration, 300 mL/min flow rate) was continuously driven at 3 Hz through the ascending tracheal tube. Mice were then head-fixed and the bone over the dorsal OB thinned. For widefield imaging experiments, a large well surrounding the dorsal OB was constructed with dental cement and securely covered with a cut glass coverslip, forming a chamber with caudal opening. This chamber was filled with Ringer’s solution to render the thinned bone transparent, yielding a cranial window with stable optical plane throughout the experiment. Epifluorescence was collected through a 4×, 0.28 N.A. air objective (Olympus) at 256×256-pixel resolution and 25 Hz frame rate using a back-illuminated CCD camera (NeuroCCD-SM256; RedShirt Imaging) and Neuroplex software, with illumination provided by a 470 nm LED (M470L2, Thorlabs) and green fluorescent protein filter set (GFP-1828A-000, Semrock). For experiments involving both widefield and two-photon imaging trials, epifluorescence was collected similar to above using a 5×, 0.25 N.A. air objective (Olympus), while two-photon fluorescence was collected with 15.2 Hz frame rate using a resonant-scanning microscope (Sutter Instruments) coupled to a pulsed Ti-Sapphire laser (Mai Tai HP, Spectra Physics) tuned to 920 nm and equipped with a 16×, 0.8 N.A. water-dipping objective (Nikon) and GaAsP photomultiplier (Hamamatsu H10770B).

For epifluorescence imaging in awake, head-fixed mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the bone overlying both OBs was thinned and sealed with cyanoacrylate (Krazy Glue) to preserve transparency and a headbar was implanted caudal to the OBs (Wachowiak et al., 2013). Beginning 3–5 days after the surgical procedure, mice were acclimated to head fixation for periods increasing from 10 to 30 min over 3–4 days. A circular treadmill (design courtesy of D. Rinberg, New York University) allowed for locomotory movements and minimized torque on the headbar. Odorant-evoked responses were imaged on the same optical setup and using the same odorant delivery paradigm as in anesthetized mice. Data were collected over 2–3 consecutive daily sessions lasting 45–60 min.

### Odorant response maps

To generate odorant response maps, raw data from the ≥3 presentations of each odorant were first averaged, then ΔF images generated by, for each pixel, subtracting the mean of the fluorescence signal in the 1 s prior to odorant delivery onset from the mean signal in seconds 2–3 after odorant delivery onset. This time-window nearly always captured the time of the peak of the signal, except in rare cases where responses began to decline before odorant offset, presumably due to adaptation of OSNs. For presentation in the Figures, the resulting ∆F response maps were clipped at zero and a maximum equal to the mean of the highest 65 pixels, smoothed slightly by convolving with a 2D Gaussian kernel (sigma: 0.75 pixels), and the pixel resolution doubled (to 512 × 512 pixels) with bilinear interpolation. Response maps were displayed in units of ∆F as these facilitated visualization of glomerular foci without amplifying noisy signal from low-fluorescence areas such as blood vessels (quantitative analyses were performed after normalization by baseline fluorescence (i.e. on ∆F/F) or by maximal response, as described below).

### Signal extraction and segmentation

For the main dataset ('1 x concentrations', widefield epifluorescence), regions of interests (ROIs) representing single glomeruli were generated using an initial automated selection process followed by manual refinement. First, maximal ∆F projections were generated from the raw (unsmoothed) ΔF response maps across all odorants and initial ROI boundaries generated using 'Find Circles' in Matlab’s Image Segmenter App, followed by the 'bwconncomp' function. This initial ROI set was manually refined by addition or adjustment based on visual inspection of the maximal projections and, in some cases, individual odorant response maps. The mean ∆F signal of all pixels from each ROI was used to generate a response matrix (ROI x odorant) for each OB.

Response matrices derived from epifluorescence data required further segmentation to minimize effects from signal spread due to scattered or out-of-focus light arising from nearby glomeruli. Rather than attempt automated segmentation (Soelter et al., 2014), we verified that responses were accurately attributed to a given ROI by visual inspection. The inspection procedure involved sorting odorant response maps in descending order of their ΔF response for a given ROI, and setting to zero any entries in the response matrix that did not correspond to clear ΔF signal foci that were centered within the ROI of interest. Signals attributable to responses in adjacent ROIs were easily distinguished with this approach. Due to the sparse nature of odorant responses, the inspection algorithm required visual inspection of, typically, 5–20 response maps per ROI. Inspection was performed blind to odorant identity. In rare cases where odorants evoked clear activity that was not easily segmented into glomerular foci (e.g. octanal response maps, Supplementary file 2), no ROI was chosen and these signals were not included for analysis. Finally, responses were normalized to their baseline (pre-odorant) fluorescence to express response magnitudes in terms of relative change (ΔF/F) and to correct for potential differences in GCaMP6s expression level across glomeruli or across mice. A caveat to ΔF/F normalization is that it is unclear whether different baseline F values reflect different expression levels or levels of spontaneous activity, which may vary across ORs and their cognate OSN populations. Thus we provide both normalized and non-normalized response matrices as raw data. This issue is moot for the majority of analyses, which already involve normalizing responses across the odorant panel.

For the 10 x concentration dataset acquired with two-photon imaging, ROIs were selected manually from maximal ΔF projections, and the resulting ΔF/F response matrices were thresholded using a modified z-score cutoff based on the variance in non-responsive odorant trials for each ROI. Variance was calculated as the standard deviation of ΔF/F response values, excluding the top 10th and bottom 5th percentiles of responses across the 185-odorant spectrum. Responses corresponding to a z-score <9 were set to zero, and the resulting thresholded response matrix was used for further analysis.

### Response matrix statistical measures

To compare response magnitudes across OBs, nonzero ΔF/F values were log-normalized to achieve a normal distribution of magnitude values, then ANOVA was performed on all values grouped by OB. Pairwise post-hoc tests (Tukey’s multiple comparison of means) were used to test for differences between OBs.

Lifetime sparseness (SL), a measure of tuning of each glomerulus across the odorant response panel, was calculated as previously (Davison and Katz, 2007; Schlief and Wilson, 2007; Pashkovski et al., 2020). For a set of responses to a single glomerulus across n odorants (R={r1, r2, … rn})

$$
S_{L}=\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{n}}*1-\frac{\sumi=1n\frac{r_{i}}{n}^{2}}{\sumi=1n\frac{r_{i}^{2}}{n}}
$$

Similarly, population sparseness (SP), a measure of sparseness of n glomerular responses to each odorant (G={g1, g2, … gn}), was calculated as

$$
S_{P}=\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{n}}*1-\frac{\sumi=1n\frac{g_{i}}{n}^{2}}{\sumi=1n\frac{g_{i}^{2}}{n}}
$$

For both measures, a value of 1 indicates maximally selective tuning (a glomerular response to only one of the 185 odorants (SL), or a single glomerulus activated by an odorant (SP), while a value of 0 indicates completely nonselective tuning, i.e., equivalent responses to all odorants or equivalent activation of all glomeruli). Paired Wilcoxon signed-ranks tests were used to test for differences in SP between left and right OB responses to the same odorant presentation.

PCA was performed separately on the response matrix of each OB after normalizing each glomerulus’s response spectrum to its maximal response. ED, a measure of the number of PCs required to explain a fraction of the variance in the response dataset, was calculated as described in Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Pashkovski et al., 2020. To compare datasets with different numbers of glomeruli (and, thus, a different maximal number of PCs), we expressed variance explained as a fraction of the total number of PCs.

### Functional identification of glomeruli

To define odorants that could be reliably used to identify putatively cognate glomeruli across OBs, we first identified odorants with reliable singular or near-singular activation of glomeruli using two criteria: no more than two glomeruli activated above a 50% ΔFmax cutoff across all imaged OBs, and activation of at least one glomerulus in at least six of eight OBs, and in each of the four mice. Next, for each potential diagnostic odorant, we identified the glomerulus maximally activated by that odorant in each imaged OB and compared the response spectra of each of these glomeruli across the full 185-odorant panel using Pearson’s correlation, taking the median of all pairwise correlations across the 6–8 OBs as a measure of consistency of response spectrum. We also measured the frequency with which the response spectrum of the maximally-activated glomerulus was the most highly correlated with that of the maximally-activated glomerulus in other OBs; this fraction reflected the reliability with which the strongest-responding glomerulus to a given odorant also identified the glomerulus with the most similar response spectrum in another OB. We defined an error ratio as 1 minus this fraction. Odorants were considered diagnostic for functionally-identified glomeruli if they had a median correlation coefficient >0.8 and an error ratio <0.2.

### Odorant classification

To facilitate visual comparison of response maps across the large odorant panel, odorants were nominally grouped according to common structural classifiers including functional group, aliphatic, aromatic or cyclic structure, heteroatom substitution, etc. Odorants with mixed features are identified as such in Supplementary file 1. Within each group, odorants were ordered according to progressive changes in particular features such as carbon chain length. The ordering process was subjective and used only for data visualization. The structural classification was used only for analysis of spatial clustering (e.g. Figure 6), as described below.

### Odorant concentrations

Concentrations are reported as estimated concentration delivered to the mouse nose based on the vapor pressure of each odorant, its dilution in liquid solvent, and prior calibrations of the olfactometer using a photoionization detector (Burton et al., 2019). We assumed that the odorant and solvent behave as an ideal mixture and that odorants reach saturated vapor concentrations in their delivery reservoir as predicted by Raoult’s Law; that is, the odorant and solvent are chemically nonreactive with each other and totally miscible at all proportions. This assumption will not hold across all odorants, but was necessary as data on activity coefficients that describe deviations from ideal behavior are extremely limited for these systems. Furthermore, calculations were based on estimated vapor pressures at 25 °C calculated using the EpiSuite ‘mpvpbp’ module (US Environmental Protection Agency, https://www.epa.gov/tsca-screening-tools/epi-suitetm-estimation-program-interface) or as reported by The Good Scents company; reported vapor pressures can vary by 30–60% depending on the source and the estimation method. Given these considerations, all reported final concentrations should be considered estimates, and are reported to one significant digit precision (Supplementary file 1).

For comparison of concentrations with prior studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we compared only odorants in common with our odorant panel. For comparison to Pashkovski et al., 2020 and (Davison and Katz, 2007), we used their reported values of 100 ppm and 10 ppm, respectively. For (Soucy et al., 2009; Chae et al., 2019) we used a value of 0.5% of saturated vapor (s.v.), based on a midway point of their reported range of 0.05–1% s.v. used in the bulk of experiments. For comparisons to Ma et al., 2012, we used the lowest reported effective dilutions of saturated vapor from the ‘GIA0512’ dataset, available at https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1117491109#supplementary-materials. The specific odorants compared along with their estimated concentrations are listed in Supplementary file 3.

### Chemical descriptor sets

Glomerular response spectra were analyzed with respect to various odorant physicochemical descriptor sets, chosen from previous studies (see Text) and processed as follows: The 'Dragon1377' set was identical to that used in Haddad et al., 2008; Saito et al., 2009; Chae et al., 2019; Gerkin, 2021 and consisted of an initial set of 1664 descriptors taken from the Dragon database (Kode Systems), 1377 of which showed non-zero variance across our odorant panel. The 'Dragon32' set consisted of the subset of 32 descriptors (a subset of the original 1664) found to optimally predict odorant-OR interactions (Haddad et al., 2008). The 'FG' descriptor set consisted of the subset of 154 descriptors defining odorant functional groups (Saito et al., 2009), 49 of which had non-zero variance across our odorant panel. The 'Alvadesc2982' set was generated from an expanded list of 5666 descriptors added to the original Dragon database (Mauri, 2020), 2982 of which showed non-zero variance across our odorant set. This descriptor set included the same descriptors used in Pashkovski et al., 2020 (2873 descriptors), with additional descriptors reflecting the larger number of odorants in our panel. For all of the above descriptor sets, descriptor values were calculated using alvadesc (Alvascience, alvaDesc version 2.0.8, https://www.alvascience.com). To normalize for differences in ranges and units across the descriptor set, values for each descriptor across the odorant panel were z-scored, as done previously (Saito et al., 2009; Chae et al., 2019; Pashkovski et al., 2020).

We also defined odorant distances using PCs of the chemical space defined by the 2982 descriptors across 2587 odorants, as performed previously (Pashkovski et al., 2020) 2548 odorants were taken from the Good Scents database and met molecular weight criteria for odorous compounds (m.w. between 50 and 300); the remaining 39 were in our odorant panel but not present in this original list and so were added. Parameter values were z-scored as above before performing PCA. The first two PCs, accounting for 39.5% of the total variance, were used to visualize odorants in chemical space (Figure 1A). We used the weighting of each odorant across the first 20 PCs, which accounted for 66% of the total variance across the odorant set, to generate a 20 × 185 matrix describing the relative position of each odorant in this reduced chemical space.

Odorant distances were also defined using binary feature keysets representing the presence or absence of a particular chemical feature. 'MACCS' keys (Durant et al., 2002), 59 (of 166 total keys) of which were present in our odorant panel, were extracted using alvadesc. The SMARTS42 key set was defined using the SMARTS chemical pattern matching language (Daylight Chemical Information Systems Inc; https://www.daylight.com/dayhtml/doc/theory/theory.smarts.html), as described in the Text. The SMARTS42 set consisted of 42 features (Table 2) which were chosen to capture substructures that are present in common-use odorants, including those in our panel (e.g. carboxyl, aldehyde or ketone group; ester bonds; aromatic rings; pyridine substructure; ortho-, meta- and para-substituted rings; a number of terpenoid scaffolds; and the explicit inclusion of single-bond aliphatic chains of lengths from 6 to 11 carbon atoms). In all of the above cases, pairwise (185 × 185) odorant distance matrices were generated for each odorant-descriptor set, using cosine distance as the distance metric for the z-scored physicochemical descriptor sets and [1 - dice similarity] for the binary feature keys.

A performance metric derived from receiver-operating characteristic analysis, an approach commonly used to evaluate the quality of predictive models for receptor-ligand interactions (Lopes et al., 2017), was used to evaluate the quality of the different physicochemical descriptor sets as models for predicting glomerular odorant responses. For a given glomerulus, an initial 'query' odorant was defined as the odorant to which that glomerulus responded at the lowest concentration (i.e. primary odorant) or, in some cases (e.g. Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) the odorant that elicited the strongest response. The remaining 184 odorants were sorted in order of increasing distance from the query odorant based on a given descriptor set, and the cumulative fraction of all odorant responses explained as a function of odorant rank was plotted, generating a model performance curve, with odorant rank as the false positive rate and fraction of responses explained as the true positive rate. This curve was compared to that derived from the measured responses, generated by sorting odorants in the order of their responsiveness. The performance metric, P, was defined as

$$
P=1-2 \frac{AUC_{response}-AUC_{model}}{AUC_{response}}
$$

where AUCresponse is the area under the cumulative response curve and AUCmodel is the area under the cumulative model performance curve. A model perfectly predicting performance had a value of 1, and chance performance had a value of 0. For measuring model performance for the 19 identified glomeruli with non-singular tuning, median response spectra across all responsive OBs were used, and the query odorant was the primary odorant, with response spectra binarized before evaluation. For comparing performance using the strongest-activating odorant, odorants were sorted in descending order of their response amplitudes and odorant number was plotted against the cumulative fraction of the summed response amplitudes explained. For measuring performance for individual glomeruli across the full dataset, responses were thresholded at 10% of the maximal response for each glomerulus, binarized, and analysis performed only on glomeruli responding above threshold to more than one odorant (694 total glomeruli). For each glomerulus, the performance metric was calculated using each effective odorant as the query odorant (rather than the primary odorant) and the median of these values was reported.

### Response matrix correlation and co-tuning analysis

Odorant response correlation matrices were generated by calculating rank correlation (Spearman’s ρ) across all glomeruli in a response matrix for all odorant pairs; the resulting odorant correlation matrices were averaged across the eight imaged OBs. Because odorant response vectors typically included only a few responsive glomeruli, we also calculated pairwise odorant co-tuning matrices using a binary measure of responsiveness, where the co-tuning index was equal to the number of glomeruli responsive to a given odorant pair, at any magnitude. Pairwise co-tuning matrices were then averaged across the eight OBs and thresholded at 0.875 (corresponding to an average of at least one co-tuned glomerulus in seven of the eight OBs) to highlight the most consistent odorant co-tuning relationships. Co-tuning relationships were then visualized as a circular network graph using the mean, thresholded co-tuning matrix as the weighted adjacency matrix input. The network graph was rendered using the 'circulargraph' function in Matlab (https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/48576-circulargraph/).

### Spatial clustering analysis

To test for nonrandom spatial distribution of glomerular odorant sensitivities, we used the spatial point pattern measure Ripley’s K, which reports whether points within a given radius, r, are dispersed, clustered, or randomly distributed (Ripley, 1977). Within each preparation, each glomerulus was assigned to an odorant group based on our structural classification of its primary odorant and Ripley’s K was calculated using the set of glomeruli in a given group. Glomeruli with primary odorants having mixed classification (16 of the 185 odorants; see Supplementary file 1) were excluded from analysis. Each imaged OB was analyzed separately and treated as a replicate for statistical analysis. A minimum of three glomeruli per structural group in each OB were required to support statistical tests; nine of the 16 groups met these criteria. For these groups, K was calculated for increasing radius (r) values from 0 to ~400 μm (depending on the largest spread of glomeruli in each dataset), in 512 steps of ~0.7–0.8 μm, using the R package ‘spatstat’ (http://spatstat.org/). Statistical significance of K at each r was calculated by comparing to a Monte Carlo distribution of K values calculated from the same number of glomeruli randomly chosen from the full glomerular array (10,000 iterations). p-values were taken directly from the probability distribution of the Monte Carlo simulation. We used an alpha level of p<0.01 to identify the radius at which nonrandom spatial distributions of glomeruli existed in each dataset; significant Ripley’s K values were always greater than the random distribution, indicating spatial clustering. To prevent over-interpreting spurious significant values of r, we further required that Ripley’s K remain significant at all increasing radii to consider spatial clustering to be meaningful at a given radius.

1) In preparing the revision, it was encouraged to focus on resolving technical questions related to the imaging preparation and associated interpretations. This pertains to the major comments of reviewer #3 and the second and third comments of reviewer #2.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

Figure 2B – The name of the odorants depicted in the figure should be described in the Figure legend.

Table S2 – Explain in the legend what the anterior-posterior and mediolateral positions mean.

Citation of some primary work is missing, for example:

https://doi.org/10.1016/S0896-6273(00)80803-X

Gilles Sicard, Andre´ Holley, Receptor cell responses to odorants: Similarities and differences among odorants, Brain Research, Volume 292, Issue 2, 1984, Pages 283-296,

https://doi.org/10.1016/0006-8993(84)90764-9

This is in frogs, but one of the first comparing odorant structural features in single olfactory neuron responses.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

In "Mapping odorant sensitivities reveals a sparse but structured representation of olfactory chemical space by sensory input to the mouse olfactory bulb", Burton et al., aim to functionally map odorant responses across the olfactory bulb dorsal surface. The authors characterized glomerular responses to a large odorant panel at low concentration ranges and derived a robust map of 25 glomeruli that are sensitive to a primary odorant. This manuscript represents an important resource to the community, however, there are some points of interpretation/analysis that require revision.

1. In the current analyses, the rationale for not fold-normalizing to the baseline is not adequately provided (given biological heterogeneity e.g., reporter expression); importantly, the δ F alone could be misleading in subsequent PCA analyses (lines 607-608). We recommend converting to a dF/F in this report.

2. The main observation that the authors emphasize is the high dimensionality of the glomerular responses to a large panel of low-concentration odorants. There are a couple of important points here. First, it is not surprising that at low concentrations dimensionality should rise, given what we know about how GPCRs work – in this sense, it is perhaps best to state this as an obvious prediction that is borne out by the data. Second, the dimensionality of neural responses to odors is the consequence of two separate things: odor concentration and the set of odors tested. The authors repeatedly point out that what they are observing is higher dimensional than what has been observed by others, despite the fact that the data being compared are nearly always querying different parts of odor space at different levels of resolution. Some clarity over this point as in the results and Discussion section would be useful – and perhaps most useful would be apples-to-apples comparisons where these authors have looked at the same odors as others. In the absence of that, it is difficult to disentangle whether the reason for the high dimensionality is because of concentration or differences in odor identity across the odor set.

3. Lines 697-700: The authors assessed how well each of these odorant-descriptor distances predict the glomerular responses. In the methods, the "model" part of this analysis is not clearly described – it seems like the authors are asking how, across glomeruli and odors, the rank order of glomerular activity observed relates to the rank order of odor distances given an odor distance metric (quantified using an auROC). If I'm understanding this correctly, this is not a "model" in the sense that nothing is fit, nothing is held out, and there is no statistical metric generated that shows the "model" output is not a consequence of chance. I'm actually cool with this way of capturing neural activity-odor distance relationships, but more description and perhaps a change in language are important for clarity. More importantly, however, the author seems to be looking at cosine distances of each descriptor set and then judging descriptor quality, despite the fact that each of these descriptor sets has its own covariance structure and thus variation in information about odor relationships is differentially distributed across dimensions. The authors mention using 20 PCs (which account for some amount of variance) for one of the odor descriptor sets. The key question here is: given an equal amount of variance captured, how do odor descriptor sets compare? It is not possible to know that answer without PCA being applied to all the descriptor sets (in the same manner that it was for that one odor set) and to then look at performance a. as a function of PCs and b. as a function of variance explained; if the 42 element SMARTS set outperforms DRAGON given an equal amount of chemical variance explained, it would mean that SMARTS is fundamentally more informative than DRAGON. Absent this kind of normalization it is hard to know why one odor descriptor set outperforms another.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dewan et al., 2018 and Williams and Dewan, 2020.

claims.claim: Initial estimated delivered odorant concentrations were set to approximately 1 pM.

claims.claim: Concentrations were systematically increased or decreased by tenfold steps up to approximately 1 nM to identify the lowest concentration for each odorant capable of reliably activating at least one glomerulus.
claims.source: Across a series of pilot experiments, concentrations were then systematically increased (or occasionally decreased) by tenfold steps up to ~1 nM to identify the lowest concentration for each odorant capable of reliably activating at least one glomerulus, with responses averaged across at least three trials (typically, four) per concentration and odorant.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: Final analyzed concentrations were identical across animals for the majority of odorants (145/185).
claims.source: Final analyzed concentrations were identical across animals for the majority of odorants (145/185), and none differed by more than tenfold across the four mice.

claims.claim: No odorant concentration differed by more than tenfold across the four mice.
claims.source: Final analyzed concentrations were identical across animals for the majority of odorants (145/185), and none differed by more than tenfold across the four mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claims.claim: 163 of 185 odorants (88%) evoked responses in one or more dorsal glomeruli per OB per mouse.
claims.source: Nearly all odorants tested proved effective within the picomolar-to-nanomolar concentration range: 163 of 185 odorants (88%) evoked responses in one or more dorsal glomeruli per OB per mouse, and only twelve odorants proved ineffective (i.e. failed to elicit a response in any OB).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data from the experiments.

claims.claim: Only twelve odorants failed to elicit a response in any OB.

claims.claim: Response amplitudes were lognormally distributed.
claims.source: Response amplitudes were lognormally distributed (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), with a mean ln(∆F/F) of 1.48 (corresponding to 4.4% ∆F/F, mean of means across 8 OBs; mean s.d. of responses: 1.03 ln(∆F/F); number of responses per OB: 308–484).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) and specific numerical data.

claims.claim: The mean ln(∆F/F) of response amplitudes was 1.48, corresponding to 4.4% ∆F/F.
claims.source: Response amplitudes were lognormally distributed (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), with a mean ln(∆F/F) of 1.48 (corresponding to 4.4% ∆F/F, mean of means across 8 OBs; mean s.d. of responses: 1.03 ln(∆F/F); number of responses per OB: 308–484).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data from the experiments.

claims.claim: Patterns of glomerular activation were remarkably consistent across all eight OBs.
claims.source: Qualitatively, patterns of glomerular activation were remarkably consistent across all eight OBs.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as a qualitative observation from the data.

claims.claim: There were only modest differences in overall response magnitudes across mice or between left and right OBs in the same mouse.
claims.source: There were only modest differences in overall response magnitudes across mice or between left and right OBs in the same mouse (ANOVA on all nonzero ∆F/F responses for each OB (F7,3385=12.97, p<2e–16); post-hoc Tukey's multiple comparisons of means: p=7e–7 for 1 of 4 left vs. right OB pairs; p>0.5 for 3 of 4 pairs); these differences likely reflect differences in nasal patency between mice or between sides.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA and post-hoc tests) with specific p-values.

claims.claim: Differences in response magnitudes likely reflect differences in nasal patency between mice or between sides.
claims.source: There were only modest differences in overall response magnitudes across mice or between left and right OBs in the same mouse (ANOVA on all nonzero ∆F/F responses for each OB (F7,3385=12.97, p<2e–16); post-hoc Tukey's multiple comparisons of means: p=7e–7 for 1 of 4 left vs. right OB pairs; p>0.5 for 3 of 4 pairs); these differences likely reflect differences in nasal patency between mice or between sides.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the observed data.

claims.claim: The cumulative number of glomeruli activated across the odorant panel ranged from 103 to 142 per OB with a median of 126.
claims.source: The cumulative number of glomeruli activated across the odorant panel ranged from 103 to 142 per OB (median: 126) and covered the extent of the dorsal OB (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A recent report mapping ORs to the OB identified approximately 130 ORs/TAARs from the same area of the OB imaged in the present study.
claims.source: A recent report mapping ORs to the OB identified ~130 ORs/trace amine-associated receptors (TAARs) from the same area of the OB imaged in the present study (Zhu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2021.

claims.claim: A range of 150–160 glomeruli is a reasonable estimate of the number of glomeruli present in the imaging area.
claims.source: Allowing for failure to detect low-abundance ORs in Zhu et al., 2021 and slight mismatches in tissue area, a range of 150–160 glomeruli is a reasonable estimate of the number of glomeruli present in our imaging area.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an inference based on data from Zhu et al., 2021 and considerations of detection limitations.

claims.claim: The odorant panel was able to identify 75–90% of glomeruli in the imaged area.
claims.source: Thus we estimate that our odorant panel was able to identify 75–90% of glomeruli in the imaged area.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an estimate based on the number of activated glomeruli and the estimated total number of glomeruli.

claims.claim: Final estimated concentrations ranged from 4 × 10–14 to 4 × 10–9 M with a median of 1 × 10–10 M (2.4 ppb).
claims.source: Across all odorants, final estimated concentrations ranged from 4 × 10–14 to 4 × 10–9 M (median: 1 × 10–10 M, 2.4 ppb) (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Maximal glomerular sensitivity had a median concentration of 2 × 10–11 M (0.5 ppb).
claims.source: Maximal glomerular sensitivity (i.e. the concentration at which each glomerulus responded to its primary odorant) was distributed across even lower concentrations, with a median of 2 × 10–11 M (0.5 ppb) (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The concentrations used are substantially lower than those used to characterize odorant representations in earlier studies, by as much as 4–5 orders of magnitude.
claims.source: These concentrations are, overall, substantially lower than those used to characterize odorant representations in earlier studies, by as much as 4–5 orders of magnitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and indicate that high odorant sensitivity is a general feature of OSN inputs to glomeruli.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2 comparing concentrations across studies.

claims.claim: High odorant sensitivity is a general feature of OSN inputs to glomeruli.
claims.source: These concentrations are, overall, substantially lower than those used to characterize odorant representations in earlier studies, by as much as 4–5 orders of magnitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and indicate that high odorant sensitivity is a general feature of OSN inputs to glomeruli.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the concentration data.

claims.claim: Each effective odorant evoked input to only a few glomeruli with a median of 2 glomeruli per odorant.
claims.source: Our experimental approach was designed to yield sparse glomerular responses to each odorant. Nevertheless, the degree of sparseness was striking, with each effective odorant evoking input to only a few glomeruli (median: 2 glomeruli per odorant; quartiles: 1–3 glomeruli per odorant; 1290 responses across 8 OBs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Population sparseness was exceptionally high with a median SP of 0.994.
claims.source: Population sparseness (SP), a measure of the selectivity of glomerular activation for a given odorant, was exceptionally high (median SP: 0.994; quartiles: 0.990–0.997, calculated from mean SP per odorant across 8 OBs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: There was no difference in SP between the left and right OBs of the same mouse.
claims.source: There was no difference in SP between the left and right OBs of the same mouse (paired Wilcoxon Signed-Ranks test, Bonferroni-corrected p-values for each of 4 mice: p=0.12, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing with specific p-values.

claims.claim: Individual glomeruli are narrowly tuned across the entire odorant panel.
claims.source: This result implies that individual glomeruli are narrowly tuned across the entire odorant panel.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the high population sparseness data.

claims.claim: Earlier characterizations of OR tuning have identified a mix of narrowly- and broadly-tuned ORs.
claims.source: Earlier characterizations of OR tuning have identified a mix of narrowly- and broadly-tuned ORs (Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Saito et al., 2009; Nara et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Saito et al., 2009; and Nara et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Narrow tuning of OSN inputs to nearly all glomeruli was observed.
claims.source: Here, we observed narrow tuning of OSN inputs to nearly all glomeruli, and for glomeruli tuned to nearly all odorants (Figure 1E and F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 1E, F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Lifetime sparseness was extremely high across the glomerular population with a median value of 0.995.
claims.source: Lifetime sparseness (SL), a measure of stimulus selectivity that reflects the distribution of response magnitudes across a stimulus set and ranges from 0 (no stimulus selectivity) to 1 (response to only a single stimulus) (Davison and Katz, 2007; Schlief and Wilson, 2007), was extremely high across the glomerular population, with a median value of 0.995 (mean of medians across 8 OBs; mean quartiles: 0.989–1) (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data, supported by Figure 1H, and references definitions from Davison and Katz, 2007 and Schlief and Wilson, 2007.

claims.claim: 25–30% of glomeruli in a given OB responded to only one odorant from the panel.
claims.source: 25–30% of glomeruli in a given OB (mean ± s.d.: 29% ± 6%, 288/1004 total glomeruli) responded to only one odorant from the panel, and only 19% of glomeruli (187/1004) responded to more than five odorants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Only 19% of glomeruli responded to more than five odorants.
claims.source: 25–30% of glomeruli in a given OB (mean ± s.d.: 29% ± 6%, 288/1004 total glomeruli) responded to only one odorant from the panel, and only 19% of glomeruli (187/1004) responded to more than five odorants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Sparse responses and narrow tuning of glomeruli was not due to an 'iceberg effect' where only a few odorants evoked responses detectable above the signal-to-noise ratio.
claims.source: Sparse responses and narrow tuning of glomeruli was not due to an 'iceberg effect', in which only a few odorants evoked responses detectable above the signal-to-noise ratio of our imaging approach, as response amplitudes were typically many times greater than baseline variance levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the observation that response amplitudes were much greater than baseline variance.

claims.claim: 75% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant had a dynamic range greater than 2.
claims.source: 75% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant (n=716) had a dynamic range (i.e. the ratio between the strongest and weakest odorant responses) greater than 2, 50% had a range greater than 4, and 20% had a range greater than 10, indicating a high dynamic range in odorant responsiveness even in this low-concentration regime.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claims.claim: 50% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant had a dynamic range greater than 4.
claims.source: 75% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant (n=716) had a dynamic range (i.e. the ratio between the strongest and weakest odorant responses) greater than 2, 50% had a range greater than 4, and 20% had a range greater than 10, indicating a high dynamic range in odorant responsiveness even in this low-concentration regime.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claims.claim: 20% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant had a dynamic range greater than 10.
claims.source: 75% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant (n=716) had a dynamic range (i.e. the ratio between the strongest and weakest odorant responses) greater than 2, 50% had a range greater than 4, and 20% had a range greater than 10, indicating a high dynamic range in odorant responsiveness even in this low-concentration regime.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claims.claim: SL values were consistently high and independent of both dynamic range and maximum response amplitude.
claims.source: SL values were also consistently high and independent of both dynamic range and maximum response amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, E), indicating that sparse responses are not an artifact of low signal-to-noise ratios or of weakly-responding glomeruli.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3D and E.

claims.claim: Sparse responses are not an artifact of low signal-to-noise ratios or of weakly-responding glomeruli.
claims.source: SL values were also consistently high and independent of both dynamic range and maximum response amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, E), indicating that sparse responses are not an artifact of low signal-to-noise ratios or of weakly-responding glomeruli.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the independence of SL values from dynamic range and response amplitude.

claims.claim: 159 odorants of the panel were presented at tenfold higher concentrations in two separate preparations using two-photon imaging.
claims.source: We further tested the concentration-dependence of OSN tuning by presenting 159 odorants of the panel at tenfold higher concentrations in two separate preparations (the remaining 26 odorants were presented at the same concentration as the widefield imaging set but omitted from this concentration-dependent analysis; see Supplementary file 1), using two-photon imaging from a central subregion of the dorsal OB in order to more precisely attribute signals to specific glomeruli (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Glomerular tuning was only slightly broader at tenfold higher concentrations, with 12% of glomeruli activated by only one of the 159 odorants and a median SL of 0.983.
claims.source: Glomerular tuning was only slightly broader at these higher concentrations, with 12% of glomeruli activated by only one of the 159 odorants and a median SL of 0.983 (quartiles: 0.973–0.994; 100 responsive glomeruli, 2 mice) (Figure 1G and H).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1G and H.

claims.claim: Narrow OSN tuning was not restricted to carefully-chosen perithreshold concentrations.
claims.source: Narrow OSN tuning was thus not restricted to carefully-chosen perithreshold concentrations, suggesting that sparse and selective glomerular activation is a robust feature of odorant representations in low-concentration regimes.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the observation of narrow tuning at higher concentrations.

claims.claim: Sparse and selective glomerular activation is a robust feature of odorant representations in low-concentration regimes.
claims.source: Narrow OSN tuning was thus not restricted to carefully-chosen perithreshold concentrations, suggesting that sparse and selective glomerular activation is a robust feature of odorant representations in low-concentration regimes.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the concentration-dependence data.

claims.claim: Previous studies examining neural responses to higher concentrations have proposed that odorant identity can be reliably encoded within a structured, lower-dimensional neural coding space.
claims.source: Previous studies examining neural responses to higher concentrations have proposed that odorant identity can be reliably encoded within a structured, lower-dimensional neural coding space (Chae et al., 2019; Si et al., 2019; Pashkovski et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chae et al., 2019; Si et al., 2019; and Pashkovski et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Glomerulus-odorant response matrices in the low-concentration datasets appeared high-dimensional.
claims.source: However, glomerulus-odorant response matrices in our low-concentration datasets appeared high-dimensional, at least in the Euclidean domain.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claims.claim: The first principal component in each OB dataset accounted for only 4–7% of the total variance.
claims.source: The first principal component (PC) in each OB dataset accounted for only 4–7% of the total variance (Figure 1I), and 54–67 PCs (44–55% of possible PCs, given 100–140 glomeruli per OB) were required to account for 90% of the response variance (Figure 1J), with similar results observed for the tenfold higher concentration two-photon dataset.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1I.

claims.claim: 54–67 PCs (44–55% of possible PCs) were required to account for 90% of the response variance.
claims.source: The first principal component (PC) in each OB dataset accounted for only 4–7% of the total variance (Figure 1I), and 54–67 PCs (44–55% of possible PCs, given 100–140 glomeruli per OB) were required to account for 90% of the response variance (Figure 1J), with similar results observed for the tenfold higher concentration two-photon dataset.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1J.

claims.claim: A comparable analysis of glomerular responses to substantially higher odorant concentrations required 21 PCs to account for 90% of the response variance in a pseudopopulation of 871 glomeruli.
claims.source: These results substantially differ from the 21 PCs required to account for 90% of the response variance in a pseudopopulation of 871 glomeruli (i.e. ~2.4% of possible PCs) in a comparable analysis of glomerular responses to substantially higher odorant concentrations (Chae et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chae et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Effective dimensionality was substantially higher in the main dataset (mean ± s.d.: 48.6±4.4, n=8 OBs) than that reported for odorant responses imaged from OB projections to piriform cortex using higher odorant concentrations (ED: 13.5).
claims.source: Effective dimensionality (ED), a measure of response covariance across a dataset (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017), was also substantially higher in our main dataset (mean ± s.d.: 48.6±4.4, n=8 OBs) than that reported for odorant responses imaged from OB projections to piriform cortex using higher odorant concentrations (ED: 13.5, n=22 odorants x 3160 axonal boutons) (Pashkovski et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by citations to Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017 and Pashkovski et al., 2020.

claims.claim: A publicly available dataset describing OSN inputs to mouse OB glomeruli was collected using near-identical imaging methods and the same OMP-IRES-tTA driver line as in the present study, but with a less-sensitive GCaMP2 reporter and higher odorant concentrations.
claims.source: To that end, we took advantage of a publicly available dataset describing OSN inputs to mouse OB glomeruli, collected using near-identical imaging methods and the same OMP-IRES-tTA driver line as in the present study, but with a less-sensitive GCaMP2 reporter and higher odorant concentrations (Ma et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The median concentration in the Ma et al., 2012 dataset was 4.3 ppm, approximately 1000x higher than in the current dataset (median: 3.4 ppb).
claims.source: We generated response matrices using the lowest effective concentrations reported in this previous study for the 31 odorants common with the current study (median: 4.3 ppm; quartiles: 1.0–15.1 ppm), which were approximately 1000 x higher than in our dataset (median: 3.4 ppb; quartiles: 0.5–25 ppb) (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and reference to Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Odorants in the higher-concentration regime activated substantially more glomeruli across the same area of the dorsal OB, with a quartile range of 2–23 glomeruli per odorant (median: 5) compared to a range of 1.4–2.9 in the current dataset (median: 1.75).
claims.source: As expected, odorants in this higher-concentration regime activated substantially more glomeruli across the same area of the dorsal OB, with a quartile range of 2–23 glomeruli per odorant (median: 5) compared to a range of 1.4–2.9 in our dataset (median of mean values across 8 OBs: 1.75; p=3 × 10–5, paired Wilcoxon Signed Ranks).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and statistical testing.

claims.claim: SL of individual glomeruli across the 31 odorants was significantly lower in the higher-concentration dataset, with a quartile range of 0.84–0.97 (median: 0.9) compared to a range of 0.97–1 in the current dataset (median: 1).
claims.source: SL of individual glomeruli across the 31 odorants was also significantly lower, with a quartile range of 0.84–0.97 (median: 0.9; n=98 glomeruli from one OB) compared to a range of 0.97–1 in our dataset (median: 1; n=273 glomeruli from 8 OBs; p=0, Mann-Whitney U test).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and statistical testing.

claims.claim: Dimensionality of the glomerular responses across the 31 odorant panel was substantially lower for the higher concentration data, with an ED of 5.3 compared to 13.2±1.1 (mean ± s.d., 8 OBs).
claims.source: Dimensionality of the glomerular responses across the 31 odorant panel was also substantially lower for the higher concentration data, with an ED of 5.3 compared to 13.2±1.1 (mean ± s.d., 8 OBs).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claims.claim: The narrow tuning of glomeruli and sparser, higher dimensional odorant response patterns directly reflect differences in how odorant information is represented in the much lower concentration regime, rather than differences in odorant panel composition.
claims.source: This comparison thus further confirms that the narrow tuning of glomeruli and sparser, higher dimensional odorant response patterns in our dataset directly reflect differences in how odorant information is represented in this much lower concentration regime, rather than differences in odorant panel composition.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the comparison with the Ma et al., 2012 dataset.

claims.claim: The narrow tuning and high sensitivity of glomeruli to their primary odorants suggests that many glomeruli can be identified simply by their response to a single diagnostic odorant delivered at low concentration.
claims.source: The narrow tuning and high sensitivity of glomeruli to their primary odorants suggests that many glomeruli can be identified simply by their response to a single diagnostic odorant delivered at low concentration.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the narrow tuning and high sensitivity data.

claims.claim: The aromatic ester phenyl acetate (~3 pM) strongly activated a single glomerulus in the central OB, with identical response spectra across the 8 OBs.
claims.source: For example, the aromatic ester phenyl acetate (~3 pM) strongly activated a single glomerulus in the central OB, with identical response spectra across the 8 OBs (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: The odorant methyl tiglate (~10 pM) strongly activated a single glomerulus in the central-medial OB in each of the 8 OBs imaged.
claims.source: Likewise, the odorant methyl tiglate (~10 pM) strongly activated a single glomerulus in the central-medial OB in each of the 8 OBs imaged; this glomerulus was also strongly- and singly-activated by ethyl, hexyl, and isopropyl tiglate, as well as trans-2-methyl-2-butenal and 2-methyl-2-pentenoic acid (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: In many cases, a single diagnostic odorant can be used to identify putatively cognate glomeruli across animals.
claims.source: These observations suggest that, in many cases, a single diagnostic odorant can be used to identify putatively cognate glomeruli across animals.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the observations of consistent glomerular activation.

claims.claim: 80 odorants passed the screen for singular or near-singular glomerular activation and reliability.
claims.source: For each of the 80 odorants passing this screen, we tested the odorant's ability to identify glomeruli across OBs by comparing the response spectrum of the glomerulus most strongly activated by that odorant across the full 185-odorant panel with that of all other glomeruli in each OB.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claims.claim: For 19 odorants, the strongest activated glomerulus identified the glomerulus with the highest-correlated response spectrum in 100% of comparisons (median correlation coefficient: 0.95±0.04).
claims.source: For 19 odorants, the strongest (or only) activated glomerulus identified the glomerulus with the highest-correlated response spectrum in 100% of comparisons (median correlation coefficient [Pearson's r] across OBs: 0.95±0.04; mean ± s.d., n=19).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claims.claim: Relaxing the criteria to allow for inherent variability yielded 22 additional odorants.
claims.source: Relaxing these criteria slightly to allow for inherent variability in responsiveness across the odorant panel – to a cutoff of 80% match between the strongest-activated and most-correlated glomerulus across OBs (error ratio <0.2; see Materials and methods) and a median correlation coefficient in response spectra of >0.8 – yielded 22 additional odorants.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claims.claim: 41 odorants from the original 185-odorant panel could serve as diagnostic probes to identify 26 unique glomeruli.
claims.source: Thus, 41 odorants from the original 185-odorant panel could serve as diagnostic probes to identify 26 unique glomeruli (Table 1; Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and reference to Table 1 and Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: Glomeruli identified with this approach appeared in a similar location on the dorsal OB, with a spatial jitter consistent with that characterized for OR-defined OSN projections.
claims.source: Notably, while spatial location was not used as a diagnostic criterion, glomeruli identified with this approach appeared in a similar location on the dorsal OB, with a spatial jitter consistent with that characterized for OR-defined OSN projections (Figure 2C; Table 1; Zapiec and Mombaerts, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 2C, Table 1, and citation to Zapiec and Mombaerts, 2015.

claims.claim: Diagnostic odorant-concentration pairs evoked singular activation of the same putatively identified glomeruli in awake, head-fixed mice at the same low concentrations.
claims.source: Diagnostic odorant-concentration pairs also evoked singular activation of the same putatively identified glomeruli in awake, head-fixed mice at the same low concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that OSNs are similarly sensitive and selective during natural odorant sampling.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: OSNs are similarly sensitive and selective during natural odorant sampling.
claims.source: Diagnostic odorant-concentration pairs also evoked singular activation of the same putatively identified glomeruli in awake, head-fixed mice at the same low concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that OSNs are similarly sensitive and selective during natural odorant sampling.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the observation of similar responses in awake mice.

claims.claim: The high selectivity and sensitivity of OSNs for their primary odorants allows for simple and robust identification of cognate glomeruli across OBs using a single odorant-concentration pair.
claims.source: Thus, the high selectivity and sensitivity of OSNs for their primary odorants allows for simple and robust identification of cognate glomeruli across OBs using a single odorant-concentration pair.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the diagnostic odorant data.

claims.claim: Individual glomeruli are sensitively and selectively tuned to a very narrow portion of odorant chemical space.
claims.source: By mapping high-sensitivity odorant responses to OB glomeruli using a large and diverse odorant panel, we found that individual glomeruli – and, by inference, their cognate ORs – are sensitively and selectively tuned to a very narrow portion of odorant chemical space.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a summary conclusion from the mapping experiments.

claims.claim: Narrow tuning leads to a sparse and apparently high-dimensional representation of individual odorants in the regime of low odorant concentrations.
claims.source: This narrow tuning leads to a sparse and apparently high-dimensional representation of individual odorants in the regime of low odorant concentrations.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the narrow tuning data.

claims.claim: The small amount of structure apparent in the coding regime was well-represented by relatively simple descriptions of chemical space derived from odorant structural features.
claims.source: At the same time, the small amount of structure that was apparent in this coding regime – both in terms of glomerular tuning and glomerular location – was well-represented by relatively simple descriptions of chemical space derived from odorant structural features.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a summary conclusion from the chemical descriptor analysis.

claims.claim: The prevalence of narrowly-tuned glomeruli and the degree of selectivity in their tuning was striking.
claims.source: The prevalence of narrowly-tuned glomeruli, and the degree of selectivity in their tuning, was striking.

results.result: The study used a 185-odorant panel covering diverse chemical space, with concentrations systematically adjusted across a >1000-fold range (sub-picomolar to nanomolar) to identify high-sensitivity odorant-glomerulus interactions. Final concentrations ranged from 4×10⁻¹⁴ to 4×10⁻⁹ M (median: 1×10⁻¹⁰ M), with concentrations identical across animals for 145/185 odorants.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7, C19, C143-C145 provide comprehensive methodological details about odorant panel design, concentration selection, and preparation procedures. The systematic approach is well-documented with specific numerical data, figures (Figure 1A, 1C), and supplementary files. The concentration range and consistency across animals are clearly reported with appropriate precision.

results.result: 163 of 185 odorants (88%) evoked responses in one or more dorsal glomeruli, with response amplitudes lognormally distributed (mean ln(ΔF/F) = 1.48). The cumulative number of activated glomeruli ranged from 103-142 per OB (median: 126), estimated to represent 75-90% of glomeruli in the imaged area based on comparison with recent OR mapping studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C18 are well-supported by specific numerical data, statistical testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, ANOVA), and figures (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The estimate of 75-90% coverage is reasonably justified by comparison with Zhu et al., 2021 data, accounting for detection limitations. The consistency across OBs is demonstrated with appropriate statistical analysis.

results.result: Maximal glomerular sensitivity had a median concentration of 2×10⁻¹¹ M (0.5 ppb), substantially lower (4-5 orders of magnitude) than concentrations used in earlier studies. These concentrations are comparable to 'ultrasensitive' TAAR OSN sensitivities and indicate that high odorant sensitivity is a general feature of OSN inputs to glomeruli.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22, C77-C80 are supported by specific concentration data (Figure 1C), systematic comparison with prior studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and appropriate citations (Zhang et al., 2013; Oka et al., 2006; Tan et al., 2010). The conclusion about general high sensitivity is well-justified by the comprehensive dataset across 185 odorants and multiple glomeruli.

results.result: Odorant responses were exceptionally sparse, with each odorant activating a median of 2 glomeruli (quartiles: 1-3). Population sparseness was exceptionally high (median SP: 0.994), and lifetime sparseness was extremely high (median SL: 0.995), with 25-30% of glomeruli responding to only one odorant and only 19% responding to more than five odorants.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C31 are strongly supported by specific numerical data, appropriate sparseness metrics (SP and SL), statistical testing (paired Wilcoxon Signed-Ranks test), and figures (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C). The definitions of sparseness measures are properly cited (Davison and Katz, 2007; Schlief and Wilson, 2007). The data consistently demonstrate narrow tuning across the glomerular population.

results.result: Sparse responses and narrow tuning were not artifacts of low signal-to-noise ratios. 75% of glomeruli responding to multiple odorants had dynamic ranges >2, 50% had ranges >4, and 20% had ranges >10. Lifetime sparseness values were consistently high and independent of both dynamic range and maximum response amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 are well-supported by specific numerical data on dynamic ranges and analysis showing independence of SL from dynamic range and response amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, E). The argument against the 'iceberg effect' is logically sound and empirically supported by the observation that response amplitudes were many times greater than baseline variance.

results.result: At tenfold higher concentrations (10x), glomerular tuning remained narrow, with 12% of glomeruli activated by only one odorant and median SL of 0.983. This demonstrates that narrow OSN tuning is not restricted to perithreshold concentrations and is a robust feature of odorant representations in low-concentration regimes.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41, C75 are supported by two-photon imaging data at 10x concentrations (Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) with specific numerical results. The conclusion about robustness is justified by the persistence of narrow tuning across a tenfold concentration range. However, only two preparations were used for the 10x concentration experiments, which is a limitation.

results.result: Glomerulus-odorant response matrices appeared high-dimensional, with the first PC accounting for only 4-7% of variance and 54-67 PCs (44-55% of possible PCs) required to explain 90% of variance. Effective dimensionality (ED: 48.6±4.4) was substantially higher than reported for higher-concentration studies (ED: 13.5 in Pashkovski et al., 2020; 21 PCs for 90% variance in Chae et al., 2019).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 are supported by PCA analysis (Figure 1I, J) with specific numerical results and appropriate comparisons to prior studies (Chae et al., 2019; Pashkovski et al., 2020; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017). The high dimensionality is consistently demonstrated across 8 OBs. The comparison accounts for differences in dataset size by expressing variance as a fraction of possible PCs.

results.result: Comparison with a publicly available dataset (Ma et al., 2012) using ~1000x higher concentrations (median: 4.3 ppm vs. 3.4 ppb) showed that higher concentrations activated substantially more glomeruli per odorant (median: 5 vs. 1.75), had significantly lower SL (median: 0.9 vs. 1.0), and lower dimensionality (ED: 5.3 vs. 13.2±1.1), confirming that narrow tuning and higher dimensionality directly reflect the lower concentration regime.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 are well-supported by systematic comparison with Ma et al., 2012 dataset using 31 common odorants, with specific numerical data, statistical testing (paired Wilcoxon Signed Ranks, Mann-Whitney U test), and reference to Supplementary file 3. The comparison effectively controls for odorant panel composition by using the same odorants, strengthening the conclusion that concentration is the key variable.

results.result: The narrow tuning and high sensitivity enabled functional identification of glomeruli using single diagnostic odorants at low concentrations. 41 odorants from the panel could serve as diagnostic probes to identify 26 unique glomeruli (representing ~15% of glomeruli on the imaged surface), with 19 odorants showing 100% match between strongest-activated and most-correlated glomeruli (median r: 0.95±0.04).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C62, C65, C115-C116, C119-C120 are strongly supported by systematic screening criteria, correlation analysis, specific numerical data, and figures (Figure 2A-C, Table 1, Supplementary file 4). The spatial consistency is demonstrated with appropriate jitter analysis consistent with OR-defined projections (Zapiec and Mombaerts, 2015). The 15% estimate is reasonably derived from 26/~160 glomeruli.

results.result: Diagnostic odorant-concentration pairs evoked singular activation of the same functionally-identified glomeruli in awake, head-fixed mice at the same low concentrations, suggesting that OSNs are similarly sensitive and selective during natural odorant sampling.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64, C133 are supported by imaging data from awake mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing consistent responses at the same concentrations. However, the data are from a limited number of glomeruli and mice (3 awake mice), and the conclusion about 'natural odorant sampling' is somewhat speculative since head-fixed conditions with artificial odorant delivery may not fully replicate natural sampling behavior.

results.result: Despite overall sparse representation, systematic co-tuning relationships were found among glomeruli sensitive to their highest-sensitivity odorants, largely reflecting straightforward structural features. The most extensive co-tuning was observed among glomeruli sensitive to amines, acids/esters/aldehydes, and pyrazines/thiazoles, likely corresponding to TAAR, class I OR, and potentially a distinct class II OR subfamily.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97, C103-C105 are supported by co-tuning analysis (Figure 4, Figure 5) and network visualization showing clear structural relationships. The inference about TAAR and class I ORs is reasonable based on established knowledge. However, the speculation about pyrazine/thiazole-tuned glomeruli representing a distinct OR subfamily requires further validation.

results.result: Models incorporating relatively simple structural features (SMARTS42 and MACCS fingerprints) were more effective at predicting glomerular co-tuning than models using larger sets of computationally derived physicochemical properties. SMARTS42 had significantly higher performance metrics than all other descriptor sets including optimized Dragon32 (p=4.0×10⁻⁷).
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C102 are well-supported by systematic comparison of multiple descriptor sets using ROC-derived performance metrics (Figure 3D-F), with appropriate statistical testing (Kruskal-Wallis test, post-hoc Dunn tests). The SMARTS42 set is clearly defined (Table 2) with 42 interpretable structural features. The conclusion is strengthened by testing across 694 co-tuned glomeruli.

results.result: Spatial clustering of glomeruli with high sensitivities to structurally similar odorants was common across nearly all tested structural classes. However, clustering arose from proximal positioning of glomeruli tuned to similar but distinct odorants rather than overlapping tuning, and was overlapping/interdigitated rather than discrete (except for carboxylic acids), consistent with a functional mosaic organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C114 are supported by point-pattern analysis (Ripley's K) showing significant clustering in 7/9 testable classes (Figure 6A, B), with appropriate statistical testing (p<0.01, Monte Carlo simulation). The mosaic organization is consistent with prior studies (Soucy et al., 2009; Chae et al., 2019). The distinction from prior discrete clustering studies (Takahashi et al., 2004; Johnson and Leon, 2007) is attributed to concentration differences, which is plausible.

results.result: Individual glomeruli are sensitively and selectively tuned to a very narrow portion of odorant chemical space, leading to sparse and apparently high-dimensional representations in low-concentration regimes. The small amount of structure in this coding regime was well-represented by simple descriptions of chemical space derived from structural features.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69, C76 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from multiple analyses (sparseness, dimensionality, chemical descriptor modeling, spatial organization). These conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive dataset and multiple converging lines of evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The current findings of narrow tuning differ from most prior studies reporting a mix of broadly- and narrowly-tuned ORs/OSNs. The likely explanation is the much lower odorant concentrations used here (several orders of magnitude lower than earlier in vivo studies and 4-6 orders lower than in vitro studies).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 appropriately contextualize the current findings relative to prior literature with extensive citations. The explanation based on concentration differences is well-supported by the systematic comparison with Ma et al., 2012 (C48-C53) and Figure 1—figure supplement 2. However, other factors (reporter sensitivity, odorant panel size) are also acknowledged as potential contributors.

results.result: The concentrations used (median: 1×10⁻¹⁰ M, 2.4 ppb) were comparable to or higher than psychophysical detection thresholds in mice and to ambient concentrations of volatile organic compounds in natural environments (0.1-10 ppb), suggesting these concentrations reflect a common operating regime of the mouse olfactory system during natural behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83, C138-C140 are supported by appropriate citations to behavioral studies (Dewan et al., 2018; Cichy et al., 2019; Williams and Dewan, 2020) and environmental measurements (Petersson, 1988; Jansen et al., 2009; Bach et al., 2020; Ruuskanen et al., 2011; Mäki et al., 2019; Dehimeche et al., 2021). The inference about ecological relevance is reasonable, though natural odor environments are complex and variable.

results.result: The narrow tuning of OSNs has implications for olfactory information processing. Canonical models relying on reduced dimensionality may be less applicable in low-concentration regimes. Instead, activation of particular glomeruli may directly encode specific odorants or small groups with shared features. Natural odors may elicit combinatorial patterns reflecting component composition, and narrowly-tuned glomeruli may facilitate recognition at trace concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C93 present speculative implications and hypotheses about information processing, supported by citations to relevant models (Chae et al., 2019; Pashkovski et al., 2020) and prior observations (Davison and Katz, 2007; Lin et al., 2006; Dunkel et al., 2014). While the speculations are reasonable given the data, they require direct experimental testing of neural coding and behavior in low-concentration regimes to be confirmed.

results.result: The heterogeneity of tuning properties implies that the selectivity of different ORs may be determined by different rule sets. Relating OR ligand binding to solved protein structures will be important for understanding the molecular basis of this heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 present reasonable inferences from the observed heterogeneity in co-tuning relationships, with appropriate citation to recent structural work (Del Mármol et al., 2021). However, these remain speculative hypotheses requiring structural and functional studies of mammalian ORs to validate.

results.result: The functionally-identified glomeruli exceed the number of OR-defined glomeruli previously characterized and provide a platform for future studies. Potential applications include probing response spectra with larger panels, examining response dynamics with faster reporters, investigating circuit transformations, and facilitating OR deorphanization through alignment with spatial transcriptomics maps.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C129 appropriately discuss prior work and future applications with relevant citations. The comparison showing 26 functionally-identified glomeruli exceeds prior characterizations (Peterlin et al., 2014; Shirasu et al., 2014; Saito et al., 2017) is supported. The proposed applications are reasonable extensions, though they represent future work rather than current results.

results.result: While absolute sensitivities may be dynamically modulated by experience and sampling behavior (supported by citations to prior studies), the authors predict that response spectra remain consistent and narrowly tuned across ethologically relevant contexts. The current datasets provide a platform for testing this prediction.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C135 acknowledge potential plasticity with appropriate citations (Verhagen et al., 2007; Eiting and Wachowiak, 2020; Jordan et al., 2018; Tsukahara et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2008; Kass et al., 2013; Bhattarai et al., 2020) but predict consistency based on limited awake mouse data. The prediction requires more extensive testing across behavioral contexts and experience-dependent manipulations.

results.result: Experiments used compound heterozygous crosses of OMP-IRES-tTA and tetO-GCaMP6s mice aged 2-6 months, with procedures approved by IACUC. The OMP-IRES-tTA expression strategy did not appear to affect OSN targeting to glomeruli.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C142, C146 provide essential methodological information with appropriate citations (Yu et al., 2004; Wekselblatt et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2014; Inagaki et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021). The statement about not affecting targeting is supported by prior reports and recent mapping data, though this was not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: Prior studies have reported mixed findings on OR tuning breadth and OSN sensitivity. Discrepancies with the current study could be explained by smaller odorant panels, less-sensitive reporters, and higher concentrations used in earlier work.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C42, C81 appropriately cite prior literature (Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Saito et al., 2009; Nara et al., 2011; Chae et al., 2019; Si et al., 2019; Pashkovski et al., 2020) and provide reasonable explanations for discrepancies. The explanations are supported by the systematic comparison with Ma et al., 2012 showing concentration-dependent effects.
